title: Evolution and genotypic characteristics of small cell lung cancer transformation in non-small cell lung carcinomas
author: Jia Zhong; Xiaoting Li; Zhijie Wang; Jianchun Duan; Wenbin Li; Minglei Zhuo; Tongtong An; Ziping Wang; Tiantian Gu; Yuyan Wang; Hua Bai; Yan Wang; Meina Wu; Zhikun Zhao; Xin Yang; Zhe Su; Xiang Zhu; Rui Wan; Jianjie Li; Jie Zhao; Geyun Chang; Xue Yang; Hanxiao Chen; Liying Xue; Xiaohua Shi; Jun Zhao; Jie Wang
text:
Abstract
Background
Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) transformation had previously been reported mainly in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutant adenocarcinoma. However, the underlying genomic profile remains unclear. Our study aimed to find the evolution and genotypic characteristic of SCLC transformation.
Methods
Thirty-one SCLC transformation patients who were initially diagnosed as non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients were included. Whole exome sequencing (WES) of both primary and transformed re-biopsy lesions was conducted on 12 patients. Clinical characteristics were analyzed using R software (v.3.6.1).
Results
Our study included 31 patients, of whom, three had lung squamous cell carcinoma, 6 patients did not carry EGFR mutations, and 30 patients received chemotherapy for SCLCs. The disease control rate (DCR) was 96.7%, and the median progression-free survival (PFS) was 4.03 months. The median time to transformation was 33.07 months, and the median overall survival (OS) was 62.08 months. Somatic mutation analysis showed that besides TP53, RB1, and EGFR, there was a high occurrence of mutations to CSMD3 and ADAMTS19, especially in the EGFR-wild type (EGFR-wt) group. Concerning mutational signature, the EGFR-mutant (EGFR-mut) transformed group favored an apolipoprotein B (APOBEC) mRNA editing catalytic polypeptide-like-associated mutation pattern (P = 0.16). DNA damage repair (DDR)-related signatures were significantly enriched in the EGFR-wt transformed group (P = 0.034). Additionally, clonal evolution analysis revealed that all patients had the same main trunk genes in the phylogenetic tree. Transformed SCLCs are not sensitive to immunotherapy, possibly due to increased tumor heterogeneity.
Conclusions
Our results indicate that the EGFR-wt patients could also transform to SCLCs, but they have different genetic features with EGFR-mut patients. SCLC-transformed patients respond to classical chemotherapy and have a better prognosis than those with classical SCLCs.
Keywords: Transformation; Neoplasms, lung; Genotyic characteristic
1. Introduction
Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) are different subtypes of lung carcinoma.1, 2, 3 Although these subtypes are different histologically, recent research4,5 indicates that they both share the same cell origins and some common driver genes. For example, alveolar type 2 cells are considered to be the source of both SCLC and adenocarcinoma (ADC – a kind of NSCLC).4,5 Genetic alteration of TP536,7 and PIK3CA8, 9, 10 give rise to either SCLC, squamous cell carcinoma (SQC – another NSCLC), or ADC. These common features seem to be prerequisites of phenotypic transformation.
Mixed SCLC and ADC with an identical molecular background can be found in a single lung cancer lesion.11 SCLC transformation in EGFR mutant (EGFR-mut) ADC was also described as an epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI) resistant mechanism in patients with ADC adenocarcinoma.12, 13, 14, 15, 16 The transformed SCLC shared the same EGFR mutation with its primary ADC lesion; it is also sensitive to the etoposide plus platinum regimen.17 Recently, SCLC transformation was found in lung adenocarcinoma after treatment of anaplastic lymphoma kinase-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (ALK-TKIs),18 immuno-checkpoint inhibitors,19 and third-generation EGFR-TKIs.20 However, the underlying genomic profile of SCLC transformation remains poorly understood.
Sutherland et al.21 reported that the inactivation of TP53 and Rb1 could efficiently transform neuroendocrine and alveolar type 2 cells into SCLCs. Pros et al.22 also showed that in patient-derived cancer cells (PDCs), RB1 inactivation in EGFR-mutant lung cancer might favor SCLC transformation under EGFR-TKIs selection pressure. Additionally, Niederst et al.15 analyzed a group of resistant EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinomas and found that RB1 was lost in 100% of the purported SCLC transformed cases, but rarely in those that remained NSCLC. Offin et al.23 reported that patients with EGFR/RB1/TP53-mutant lung cancers were at high risk of small cell carcinoma transformation (7 of 39, 18%). Niederst et al. knocked down RB1 by shRNA in PC-9 and HCC-827 (two EGFR-TKI sensitive NSCLC cell lines with TP53 mutation), but they failed to alter sensitivity to EGFR-TKI, and also could not yield acquisition of neuroendocrine marker expression or SCLC morphology.15 In this case, loss of TP53 and RB1 function may not be sufficient for SCLC transformation.
In this study, we verified the SCLC transformation process via a cohort of NSCLC phenotype transformation cases, and elucidated the clinical characteristics and molecular signatures of patients with transformed SCLCs.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Patient selection
We collected clinical data from NSCLC patients who had re-biopsies in the period from June, 2011 to May, 2021 in Beijing University Cancer Hospital and Cancer Hospital of Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences. Thirty one patients, initially diagnosed as NSCLC, transformed to SCLC after treatment. All slides and tissue samples were obtained with prior informed consent approved by the Ethical Committees of the two hospitals. The clinical factors, including gender, age, histology, smoking history, and EGFR mutation status were recorded. Histological diagnosis was confirmed by two independent pathologists using tumor slides before and after the transformation. Three of the 31 patients had had surgery before the start of the research, and their primary NSCLC lesions were subjected to continuous pathology review via slide reexamination. The responses were categorized as complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable disease (SD), or progressive disease (PD) according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST 1.1). Progression-free survival (PFS) was calculated from the start of a certain treatment until the date of the first documented PD or death. Overall survival (OS) was calculated from diagnosis until the date of death. Time to transformation (TTT) was calculated from diagnosis as NSCLC until the date of pathology-confirmed SCLC transformation.
2.2. DNA preparation
Genomic analysis on tissue and blood samples from the patients before and after SCLC transformation was performed, as described below. Tumor DNA was extracted using Qiagen AllPrep DNA kits (Qiagen, China). Blood samples were collected in anti-coagulation tubes; plasma DNA was extracted using Qiagen DNA blood mini kits (Qiagen, China).24
2.3. EGFR mutation analysis and qualitative control
All tissue samples included in the study were required to have ≥15% tumor content. Extracted DNA from tissues and matched blood samples were analyzed under identical conditions to normalize detection probability. There were two methods to confirm the EGFR status: the denaturing high-performance liquid chromatography (DHPLC) using the Transgenomic Wave Nucleic Acid Fragment Analysis System with a DNA Sep column (Transgenomic, Omaha, NE), and the amplification-refractory mutation system (ADx-ARMS®; Amoy Diagnostics Co., Ltd, Xiamen, China). Both methods were employed to screen EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 substitution mutations in lung adenocarcinoma samples.
2.4. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) and mutation analysis
WES for tumor and matched blood samples from all patients was performed on an Illumina Nova6000 using 2 × 150 bp pair-end sequencing. The average data output was about 100 × coverage. FASTQ data from sequencing tumor and normal samples were first aligned to the hg19 UCSC reference genome using BWA (v0.7.12). SAM files were then converted to BAM format using Samtools (v1.9), and subsequently deduped and sorted using Picard (v2.18.22). Basic quality recalibration and indel realignment were performed using GATK (v4.0.12.0).
Variant calls were generated using GATK4 Mutect2 (v4.0.12.0). Single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and short indels were annotated using in-house annotation software with dbNSFP. ExaC, 1,000 Genomes, COSMIC, and dbSNP 138 were also used for variant annotation. Somatic variant calls were filtered using the following steps: (1) any variant identified by the 1000 Genomes Project and ExAC with a frequency greater than or equal to 0.05 was excluded, (2) variants not in the hotspot cosmic database were subtracted.
2.5. Mutational signature analysis
The mutational signature analysis was aimed at extracting different combinations of mutation types, termed as ‘signatures’, which are generated from different mutational processes. According to the nucleotides preceding (5’) and succeeding (3’) the mutated base, SNVs in exons were divided into 96 types. The extracted signatures were also compared single base substitution (SBS) signatures from Cosmic Mutational Signatures (Version 3 - May 2019) for validation. SBS1 and SBS4 signatures were defined as age and smoking, respectively, while the APOBEC signature was the sum of weigh of SBS2 and SBS13, and the DNA damage repair (DDR) signature was the sum of weights of SBS3, SBS6, SBS9, SBS10b, SBS15, SBS20, SBS21, and SBS26. The weights of each mutational signature contributing to an individual tumor sample were determined using the deconstructSigs package.25
2.6. Copy number variations analysis
The somatic copy number variants (SCNVs) were called using the CNV kit (v0.8.1) read-depth algorithm, which uses both targeted reads and nonspecifically captured off-target reads to infer copy numbers evenly across the genome. We then evaluated the frequencies and amplitudes of observed events to identify the likely driver SCNVs by GISTIC2.0.
2.7. Tumor evolution analysis
We estimated tumor purity using Allele-Frequency-based Imputation of Tumor Purity (All-FIT), which is an iterative weighted least squares method for estimating specimen purity based on the allele frequencies of variants detected in high-depth, targeted, clinical sequencing data. We then used the Pyclone model to calculate the cancer cell fractions of all samples with the purity estimated by All-FIT and copy numbers estimated by the CNV kit. If a somatic mutation was shared by all tumor tissue samples, it was defined as a trunk mutation. Otherwise, it was called a branch mutation. We then constructed tumor evolution models by in-house script based on trunk and branch mutations detected in NSCLC samples and matched transformed SCLC samples.
2.8. Tumor heterogeneity
To analyze tumor heterogeneity (temporal heterogeneity), we defined the mutations common to the samples before and after transformation as trunk mutations, and the private mutations in each sample as branch mutations. The proportion of branch mutations versus all mutations was defined as tumor heterogeneity.
2.9. Data for comparison and statistical analysis
We used the somatic mutation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas Lung Adenocarcinoma Study (TCGA-LUAD, n = 567), the statistics of mutational genes of ADC from the CHOICE study (n = 128),28 and the somatic mutation data of a Chinese cohort of SCLC patients (n = 99)29 for comparative analysis on our data. Fisher's exact test was performed for statistical analysis to compare results of different data sets. Comparison of values between different signatures was performed with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. P values < 0.05 and Q values ≤ 0.1 were considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed in the R statistical computing environment v3.6.1 (http://www.r-project.org).
3. Results
3.1. Samples and clinical data description
A total of 31 patients, initially diagnosed with NSCLC and transformed into SCLC after treatment, were enrolled in this study (Fig. 1; Supplementary Fig. 1). The pre- and post-transformed tissues of nearly all of these patients accepted immunohistological analysis (Supplementary Table. 1). All the slides were continuously reviewed by two independent pathologists. The median age was 61 (range: 27‒74) years. Our study included 15 males and 16 females. Of the 31 patients, 26 were diagnosed with lung ADC, three had lung SQC, and two had lung adenosquamous carcinoma (AD-SQC) (Table 1). Six patients were EGFR-wt, and 25 patients had EGFR sensitive mutations (10 patients had a deletion on exon 19, whereas 13 had the point mutation L858R on exon 21; one had the point mutation L861Q on exon 21, and one patient showed point mutation G719X on exon 18). Twenty-two of the 31 patients were never-smokers and 12 had adequate tissue samples for WES. Pre-transformed tumors and matched post-transformed samples from 7 patients were collected. The other 5 patients had only pre-transformed (Pt4 and Pt11) or post-transformed (Pt3, Pt12, and Pt13) samples (Fig 1 and Table 1).

All of the 25 EGFR-mut NSCLC patients, including one with lung SQC, received EGFR-TKI therapy. The total EGFR-TKI treatment time, including the first, second, and the sequenced third-generation TKI treatment time, was defined as EGFR-TKI PFS. The median EGFR-TKI PFS of EGFR-TKI recipients was 14.63 months (range: 0.93‒78.43 months). Thirty patients received chemotherapy after SCLC transformation (median PFS: 4.03 months; range: 0.73‒7.40 months). Among them, 28 patients received etoposide plus platinum, one received irinotecan plus platinum and one received etoposide monotherapy due to poor performance status. Of them, three were administered EGFR-TKIs concurrently but this therapy failed to improve PFS (chemotherapy: 4.03 months vs chemotherapy plus TKI: 5.10 months, P = 0.949). One patient received atezolizumab concurrently, but the PFS was only 0.73 month. Moreover, three patients received single-agent programmed death-1 (PD-1) inhibitor in third or beyond line. The PFS was 1.10, 0.73, and 2.33 respectively. Nineteen of the 31 patients reached the OS endpoint, and the median OS was 62.08 months (range: 18.73‒189.33 months). The median time from diagnosis to transformation was 33.07 months (range: 4.47‒98.43 months), and the median time from transformation to death was 11.03 months (range: 1.30‒141.33 months). Pt6 had the third biopsy after the progression of the EC regimen. The histology indicated transformation back to adenocarcinoma. Serial sectioning of the surgically removed and paraffin-embedded primary tumor of each of the three patients failed to reveal mixed SCLC and NSCLC.
3.2. Somatic mutations
To understand the transformation process, we performed WES on the tumors collected from 12 patients. A total of 3,790 coding mutations were detected at the ratio of 2.6:1 of nonsynonymous to synonymous events. The mean tumor mutation burden (TMB) was 5.7 mutations per megabase (lower-to-upper range: 1.44‒12.53). Seven of the 12 patients had an EGFR sensitive mutation in the pretreatment NSCLC samples, consistent with the EGFR mutation status detected earlier. Notably, five (Pt2, Pt5, Pt6, Pt8, and Pt9) of the seven EGFR-mutant patients also had EGFR mutations after SCLC transformation. Patient Pt4 was an exception to this and did not have adequate post-transformation tissue for EGFR detection, and Pt7 did not have an EGFR mutation in the post-transformation SCLC sample after a long-time (17.07 months) EGFR-TKIs exposure. Based on the EGFR mutation states upon diagnosis of NSCLC, we divided the 12 patients with adequate tissue samples into an EGFR-mut group and an EGFR wild-type (EGFR-wt) group. The mutational landscape with recurrent genes and the patients’ clinical information are shown in Fig. 2.
Except for Pt2, all patients exhibited TP53 and/or RB1 mutations, which was consistent with the results of Offin et al.23 In the pre-transformation samples, the mutation rates of TP53 and RB1 were 77.8% (7/9) and 44.4% (4/9), respectively, and the incidence of TP53 and RB1 co-mutation was 22.2% (2/9). In the post-transformation samples, the mutation rates of TP53 and RB1 were 90% (9/10) and 60% (6/10), respectively, and the incidence of TP53 and RB1 co-mutation was 60% (6/10).
We found co-mutations of CSMD3 and ADAMTS19 genes in the post-transformed samples in the EGFR-wt group. CSMD3 is a reported driver gene in SCLC, and the CSMD3 mutation frequency in SCLC was reported to be 43% in the Chinese population in April 2016.26 Reportedly, loss of CSMD3 function may contribute to the carcinogenic transformation of airway epithelial cells. ADAMTS19 encodes a member of the ADAMTS protein family (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motif), and the epigenetic loss of ADAMTS19 is associated with metastatic spread of colorectal cancer.27 Overall, all transformed EGFR-wt samples harbored missense mutations in CSMD3 and ADAMTS19. In Pt10, in particular, co-mutations in the two genes were detected in samples collected both before and after transformation. However, we did not detect co-mutations in CSMD3 and ADAMTS19 in the TCGA and other SCLC data sets. This suggests role of CSMD3 and ADAMTS19 in the EGFR-wt group during tumor transformation.
3.3. Mutational signatures
To understand the process of transformation, we performed mutational signature analysis on all samples from the 12 patients. The EGFR-mut and EGFR-wt groups showed different mutation signatures, suggesting different mutation patterns in their tumor evolution processes (Fig. 3). Recent studies indicated that a subclass of APOBEC cytidine deaminases, which converts cytosine to uracil during RNA editing and retrovirus or retrotransposon restriction, may induce mutations more frequently in solid tumors and are mainly associated with C>T or C>G transition events occurring in TCW motif (the mutated cytosine (C) is underlined; where, indicated by “W”, corresponds to either adenine (A) or thymine (T).28 In our data, the EGFR-mut group samples favored the APOBEC-associated mutation pattern, as reported by Wang et al. (2018).29 Particularly, the transformed SCLC of Pt2 had an APOBEC-related signature of about 40%, and the proportion of C>G mutations in Pt2 was higher than that of other samples. Coincidentally, the mutation load of this sample was higher than that of other samples.
DDR pathways play a key role in cancer development.30 Several DDR-related signatures were detected in our dataset, including homologous recombination repair and mismatch repair (HRR-MMR) and HRR and base excision repair (HRR-BER) (Supplementary Fig. 2). DDR-related signatures were enriched in the EGFR-wt group in post-transformed samples (P = 0.034), with two of three samples carrying these signatures. However, no post-transformed samples in the EGFR-mut group exhibited these signatures. This indicates a potential role of DDR pathways in the transformation of EGFR-wt patients.
3.4. The evolutionary process of transformation
We further analyzed the mutated genes in the samples before and after transformation and inferred the clonal evolutionary relationship of patients with paired pre-transformation and post-transformation samples (n = 7). Among them, six patients carried an EGFR mutation, and one patient (Pt10) was EGFR wild type. EGFR truncal mutations were found in five out of six EGFR-mut patients. Six patients, except Pt2, carried TP53 truncal mutations; of these patients, two developed RB1 truncal mutations, and one had an RB1 branched mutation in his post-transformation sample. Pt6 experienced histological transformations (Fig. 3B) twice. The results of clonal evolution analysis showed an evolutionary relationship between the three tissue samples, thus suggesting that the patient's transformed samples evolved from a single main clone (Fig. 3). Based on the analysis of the clonal evolution patterns of all patients, the main clone driver gene mutations (EGFR, TP53, RB1, etc.) are present in the pre-and post-transformed samples. All the shared mutations have higher variant allele frequencies in both components. In other words, the presence of an early mutation event implies that these tumors are of monoclonal origin (transformed rather than two coexisting phenotypes).
3.5. Comparison with other cohorts
To determine whether there is a specific difference in the genomic characteristics of our transformation cohort and other research cohorts, we downloaded the mutation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas lung adenocarcinoma study (TCGA-LUAD, n = 567), the CHOICE study (n = 128),31 and a separate Chinese cohort of SCLC patients (n = 99)32 for comparative analysis. In addition to EGFR (87.5% vs 11.6%, P < 0.0001), RB1 (37.5% vs 6.5%, P = 0.014), IGHMBP2 (25% vs 1.9%, P = 0.012), and ARHGEF12 (25% vs 3.4%, P = 0.031) showed significant differences in mutation frequencies between pre-transformation lung ADC samples in our study (pre-ADC, 8 cases) and TCGA-LUAD samples (567 cases). EGFR (87.5% vs 38.38%, P = 0.008), IGHMBP2 (25% vs 0.78%, P = 0.009), and RB1 (37.5% vs 4.69%, P = 0.01) also have statistically significant differences between our pre-ADC findings and those of the CHOICE study. Moreover, compared with the EGFR mutation group samples (7 cases) and the TCGA-LUAD EGFR mutation samples (66 cases), mutated genes LTBP4 (28.6% vs 3%, P = 0.0435) and MYCBP2 (28.6% vs 3%, P = 0.0435) were significantly different in the two groups. However, RB1 (42.9% vs 12.1%, P = 0.065) showed a weak statistical difference; TP53 (71.4% vs 54.5%, P = 0.456) had no significant difference in the transformed EGFR mutation samples (all gene comparative results are shown in Supplementary Table 2). The mutations of the pre-transformation samples and the TCGA-LUAD samples had significant differences in age (P = 0.00018), smoking status (P = 0.0046), and DDR (P = 0.05) signatures; the APOBEC signature had no significant differences (Supplementary Fig. 3A).
Comparing the CNV data of 8 ADCs pre-transformation samples and ADCs from the CHOICE study, we found that few shared genes are amplified or deleted, and thus, the CNV patterns are different. In the transformed ADC samples, the significantly (Q ≤ 0.1) amplified regions are 11q13.1 and 1q21.2, including the DDR-related gene MUTYH (Fig. 4A); the significantly deleted regions are 8p23.1 and 10q26.3, including DDR-related genes PMS2, ERCC5, BRCA2, POLG, BLM, WRN, and RAD17 (Fig. 4B). According to the above results, the CNV pattern of transformed samples is different from that of non-transformed lung ADC samples.
For the transformed SCLC samples, compared to the classic SCLC of the Chinese population, there are 35 mutant genes that are statistically different, of which the most significant are EGFR (60% vs 4%, P = 1.90E-05), PIK3CA (20% vs 1%, P = 0.022), and STAG2 (20% vs 2%, P = 0.041). The most significant mutational signature between our post-transformation samples and the classic Chinese population of SCLC samples is APOBEC (P = 0.0013). Other signatures are not significantly different (Supplementary Fig. 3B). However, the differences that do exist indicate that the genetic features of transformed SCLC samples may be different from classical SCLC samples.
3.6. Biomarkers for immunotherapy
Single-agent PD-1/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) antibodies showed limited benefit in SCLC treatment,33 or in transformed SCLCs.23 Therefore, we attempted to explore immunotherapy-related biomarkers in our transformed patients. There were no differences in TMB (Tumor mutational burden) levels between pre-transformed tumors and post-transformed tumors (Fig. 4C). Analysis of tumor temporal heterogeneity before and after transformation revealed that increased tumor heterogeneity after transformation (P = 0.031) might be one of the reasons for the poor immune efficacy (Fig. 4D).
4. Discussion
SCLC transformation was first reported in EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients who were resistant to EGFR-TKIs.13 Subsequently, other case reports and research also described this phenomenon.14, 34, 35, 36 However, it remains unclear whether transformation exists. SCLC and NSCLC were traditionally regarded to have different origins.5 Type 2 (SPC-expressing) cells, which were commonly deemed to give rise to adenocarcinoma, can also lead to a typical SCLC phenotype via TP53 and Rb1 inactivation.37 Furthermore, some of the same driver genes exist in both SCLC and NSCLC, such as TP537 and PIK3CA.8,10 The common cell origin and driver genes make the transformation process plausible. In our study, phylogenetic trees in the evolutionary analysis showed that all the patients shared the same trunk genes, indicating the common origins of the pre- and post-transformed tissues. Additionally, serial sectioning of the primary tumors from three patients failed to show mixed SCLC. Moreover, the EGFR mutation status of the patients’ NSCLC primary lesions and transformed SCLC lesions was consistent. Finally, the median OS was 62.08 months for these patients. This long survival time conforms to the biological behavior of NSCLC. A second primary SCLC tumor or mixed SCLC and NSCLC should be more aggressive. Overall, phenotype transformation indeed exists, and the transformed SCLC has unique clinical and genomic characteristics.
In previous studies, SCLC transformation was mainly reported in EGFR-TKI resistant lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR sensitive mutation.15,22,23,38 To our knowledge, Le et al.39 first reported transformed SCLC without EGFR-TKI exposure. Our study indicates that lung cancers that do not harbor EGFR mutations might also undergo histologic transformation independent of exposure to kinase inhibitors. However, the EGFR-wt transformed patients showed different genomic signatures. We found co-mutation of CSMD3 and ADAMTS19 in EGFR-wt transformed samples. CSMD3 is a reported driver gene in SCLCs,25 and the epigenetic loss of ADAMTS19 is associated with the metastatic spread of colorectal cancer.26 The co-mutation of both genes indicated their potential role in EGFR-wt NSCLCs during SCLC transformation. Concurrently, the EGFR-wt groups favored the DDR-related mutation signatures in the tumor evaluation process, which is different from those of the EGFR-mutant patients. Engelman et al.15 suggested transformation to SCLC is more common in EGFR-mutant tumors treated with EGFR-TKIs than in EGFR-wt cancers. Our study confirmed this finding that 26 of the 31 transformed SCLC tumors were EGFR-mut tumors. We also found that the histological evolution can occur independently of EGFR status. SCLC transformation can occur under various treatment pressures such as treatment with EGFR-TKIs, ALK-TKIs,40 immunotherapy,41 or chemotherapy.
In this study, the median time from NSCLC diagnosis to SCLC transformation was 33.07 months. SCLC transformation is a complex pathological process that takes a long time and involves multiple genomic changes. The clinical behavior of transformed SCLCs mimics classic SCLCs in respect of treatment response. Most patients responded to the platinum-etoposide regimen, and the median PFS (4.03 months in our study) was also similar to classic SCLCs. However, the transformed SCLC patients are different from classic SCLC patients in some respects. Transformed patients seem to have a better prognosis; their median OS was 62.08 months. One patient even transformed back to adenocarcinoma (Pt6). The original EGFR mutation was maintained in transformed SCLC tissues. PIK3CA and STAG2 mutations were also found to have distinguishing signatures in transformed SCLC cases.
Although transformed SCLCs have EGFR sensitive mutations, they are insensitive to EGFR-TKIs. Some co-exist genetic alterations might be the reason for the resistance. In Yu's study,42 three of the four SCLC transformed patients had MET amplification and/or T790M. In our study, mutations in EGFR bypass signaling, such as PIK3CA, AKT1, TSC1, TSC2, MTOR somatic mutations, and ERBB2 amplification, and PTEN loss, were also commonly found in transformed SCLC. The activation of EGFR bypass might be the reason for the EGFR-TKI resistance of transformed SCLCs.
Inactivation of TP53 and RB1 has long been known to induce tumorigenesis of SCLCs.15, 21 For instance, RB1 was lost in each of the 9 SCLC transformed cases in Engleman et al.’s research.15 In a Chinese cohort of transformed SCLC patients, the most common mutations were also TP53 (17/25, 68.0 %) and RB1 (9/25, 36.0 %).38 In this study, TP53 or RB1 mutation was also commonly found in pre-transformation tissues; only one transformed patient had no TP53/RB1 mutations. However, although this mutation was commonly found in our transformed tissues, TP53 and RB1 inactivation do not exist in all the transformed patients. On the other hand, EGFR-mut adenocarcinoma cell lines with TP53 loss and RB1 knockdown do not develop the SCLC phenotype.15 Therefore, the concomitant inactivation of TP53 and RB1 is not sufficient to cause NSCLCs to transform into SCLCs. Some other genomic contexts in which SCLC transformation is favored to have been identified, such as the activation of PI3K/AKT and NOTCH pathways.43 We also found such genomic features of SCLC transformed patients beyond TP53 and RB1 mutations. In our study, IGHMBP2 and ARHGEF12 also more frequently occur in transformed patients. The APOBEC mutation signature was also found in SCLC transformed patients, as previously reported.16 To our knowledge, the present study is the first to report the DDR mutation signatures. It was commonly found in transformed patients, especially those with wild-type EGFR.
A previous study indicated that transformed SCLC tumors do not respond to immunotherapy.17 In our study, the transformed SCLCs also had a poor response to immunotherapy either in monotherapy or combined therapy. In analyzing the heterogeneity of tumor tissue before and after transformation, we found increased tumor heterogeneity after transformation. This may be one of the reasons for the poor immune efficacy.
In summary, we conclude that the transformation process can occur independently of EGFR status, without EGFR-TKI exposure. The EGFR-mut transformed tumor had different genomic characteristics compared with their EGFR-wt counterpart. This study also reveals the clinical characteristics of transformed patients. Multicenter studies are required to better elucidate optimal strategies for patients that have experienced or are experiencing this important but uncommon phenotypic transformation.
